items.text: Round 1 decisions synthesized into plan: (d1) releases stay in deployments/ package, (d2) SELECT FOR UPDATE for supersede locking, (d3) full CRUD handlers, (d4) released_by column included as nullable. All aligned with existing codebase patterns.
Validation report flagged 3 issues: missing 'Rollout/Validation Checklist' section, no greenfield declaration, no 'vrooli scenario restart' final step. These will be added to plan.md this round.

items.topic: Go type null handling strategy for optional fields
items.context: The research Finding 10 uses plain Go strings (e.g., `DeploymentID string`) with omitempty JSON tags. But the existing approvals code uses sql.NullString/sql.NullInt64/sql.NullTime with helper functions for scanning. Using plain strings would diverge from the established pattern and cause scan errors when columns are NULL.

options.label: Use sql.Null* types (match existing pattern)
options.rationale: Consistent with approvals_types.go and published_versions.go. Works correctly with database NULL values. The existing helper functions (nullStringValue, etc.) already handle JSON serialization. Recommended because consistency reduces cognitive load and avoids scan bugs.

options.label: Use pointer types (*string, *time.Time)
options.rationale: Cleaner JSON serialization (nil → omitted, vs sql.NullString needing custom marshaling). Common Go idiom. But diverges from every other type in the deployments/ package.

options.label: Other
options.rationale: Provide your own null handling approach.

items.topic: Test setup: shared helpers vs self-contained
items.context: The existing test infrastructure lives in api/server/ (integration_test.go, main_test.go with testcontainers). The releases repository tests need a running postgres with the releases schema + dependent tables (profiles, deployments, deployment_approvals). Two approaches exist in the codebase: server-level integration tests (server/integration_test.go) and package-level tests (orchestrator_test.go mocks its deps).

options.label: Add repository integration tests in deployments/ using testcontainers directly
options.rationale: Self-contained: the package owns its test DB setup. Runs migrations 002-005 in setup. Follows the same testcontainers pattern but scoped to the package. Recommended because it tests the SQL layer in isolation without requiring the full server.

options.label: Add tests only in server/integration_test.go alongside existing server tests
options.rationale: Reuses the existing test infrastructure and DB setup. But couples release repo tests to the full server lifecycle and makes test isolation harder.

options.label: Both: unit tests with mocks in deployments/ + integration in server/
options.rationale: Maximum coverage. But the repository layer is thin SQL wrappers where mocks add little value — the real test is the SQL.

items.context: The Orchestrator (orchestrator.go) is created with NewOrchestratorFull(profilesRepo, approvalsRepo, publishedVersionsRepo, logFn). When releases are wired in, it will need a releasesRepo parameter too. However, the description says orchestrator integration is a separate backlog item. The question is whether to add the repo parameter now (unused) or leave the orchestrator untouched.

options.label: Add releasesRepo to Orchestrator constructor now, but don't use it yet
options.rationale: Avoids a follow-up refactor of the constructor signature. The orchestrator already takes 4 params — adding a 5th is trivial. The field sits unused until the integration task. Recommended because it's low-effort and prevents a breaking change later.

options.label: Leave Orchestrator untouched — integration task handles it
options.rationale: Strict scope separation. This task's Definition of Done doesn't mention the orchestrator. Clean boundary between 'data layer' and 'integration' tasks.

items.context: The plan mentions a 'limit' query param for ListByProfile. The existing published-versions endpoint doesn't paginate (returns all). For releases, which could accumulate over time, a pagination strategy is needed.

options.label: Simple limit+offset with defaults (limit=50, offset=0)
options.rationale: Standard REST pagination. Easy to implement. Sufficient for typical release counts per profile (likely < 1000). Recommended because it's simple and covers the use case without premature optimization.

options.label: Cursor-based pagination (keyset on created_at)
options.rationale: More performant for large datasets and consistent with append-only data. But adds complexity for marginal benefit given expected data volume.

options.label: Limit only (no offset), like published_versions
options.rationale: Simplest possible. Just a cap on results. Consistent with existing endpoint. But no way to page through older releases.
